q: An Italian producer's name is preceded by Azienda Agricola on one bottle and by Azienda Vinicola on another. What separates the two descriptions?
opts: The agricola is simply the older of the two company forms
The agricola is a co-operative and the vinicola a private company
The agricola farms its own vineyards; the vinicola need not
The agricola may bottle only wine of the highest denomination
exp: Agricola describes a farming business, so the fruit comes off land the company works. Vinicola describes a winemaking business with no farming requirement behind it at all, which means the grapes may have been bought from anyone. Either word tells a buyer more than any adjective on the front of the bottle.

q: A guest points at the words Cellared and bottled by on an American back label and asks whether the winery named there made the wine. What has that winery not done?
opts: Carried out the fermentation of the wine
Blended the wine before it was bottled
Held and matured the wine before bottling
Filtered or fined the wine in the cellar
exp: The phrase covers wine bought in already made and then held, blended or matured before bottling. American rules keep a separate and stricter form of words for a winery that did the fermenting itself at the address printed, so cellared is what is left when that work was done elsewhere. The winemaking that shaped the wine was somebody else's.

q: One bottle names a domaine and another a merchant house, and both carry the same appellation and vintage. Which question does the domaine name answer that the merchant name leaves open?
opts: How long the wine was aged
Which year the fruit was picked and pressed
How many bottles were made
Who farmed the vines
exp: A domaine bottles wine from land it works, so the name on the glass is also the name of the farmer. A merchant's trading name guarantees a house style and an address, and says nothing about who pruned, who picked or who decided the harvest date.

q: No turret, no manor and no gatehouse stand anywhere on the property, and yet the label reads Chateau. Is that legitimate?
opts: Yes; on a wine label the word marks a defined holding whose wine is made on site, not a building
Yes, but only for wines from Bordeaux
No; the word is reserved for estates ranked in the 1855 classification
No; the word may be used only where a building of listed historic standing survives on the property
exp: European rules treat the term as tied to a vineyard holding: the fruit has to come from that holding and the wine has to be made there. A modest farmhouse therefore qualifies while a grand house buying its grapes in does not, so the word describes production and not architecture.

q: The largest words on a supermarket bottle are a coined two-word phrase that appears in no atlas and in no statute. What is that phrase?
opts: An appellation of origin
A brand name owned by the producer or the retailer
The name of a vineyard
A protected traditional term recognised across the European Union
exp: Type size is a marketing decision rather than a hierarchy, so the biggest words on a label are very often the element with the least legal content behind them. The origin claim may sit at half the size beneath, and it is the one that actually binds anybody to anything.

q: Two place names compete for attention on an unfamiliar label. Which clue most reliably marks the one that is the appellation?
opts: The name that is also repeated on the capsule
The name set in the larger type of the two
The name printed closest to the vintage, since the year and the origin are required to sit together
A legal designation printed with it, such as Denominacion de Origen or Appellation Controlee
exp: Size and position are design choices that change from bottle to bottle, and a capsule or a neck band is no better a guide, but an appellation is usually printed with the formula that gives it force. The habit is not universal: Champagne needs no Appellation Controlee line because the word itself is the appellation, German labels carry Qualitatswein or a Pradikat instead, and an American AVA stands on its own. The other place name is usually the estate, a vineyard, or a brand borrowing local colour.

q: A producer line reads Cave Cooperative on one bottle and Cantina Sociale on another. What kind of business is named in each case?
opts: A public body that approves wine before release
A winery jointly owned by its member growers
A family estate trading under a formal company name
A merchant buying finished wine and blending it under its own name
exp: The members own the winery between them and bring their grapes to it, so a single name can stand for hundreds of separate holdings. Co-operatives make a very large share of the wine in many regions, and their range runs from bulk through to serious single-site bottlings.

q: Millesime on a French label, Jahrgang on a German one and Annata on an Italian one all introduce the same piece of information. What is it?
opts: The number of bottles produced
The year the grapes were harvested
The year the wine was bottled
The age of the vines
exp: A vintage is fixed at the harvest, so a wine picked in one year and released four years later still carries the picking year. Cosecha does the same work in Spanish, and none of these words says anything about when the bottle was actually filled.

q: A long official number runs along the bottom of a German label and its final two digits read 21, while the front of the bottle says 2019. What do those last digits record?
opts: The batch number within the estate's own records
The alcoholic strength rounded to a whole number
The year the wine passed its official test
The year the grapes were harvested
exp: Germany's official test number is granted once a wine has passed analysis and a tasting panel, and it ends with the year that happened. A wine submitted after the turn of the year therefore carries a number that looks like a later vintage, which catches out anyone reading the small print in place of the front label.

q: No year appears anywhere on a bottle of inexpensive branded red. What does the absence tell a buyer about the contents?
opts: The wine lost its year when it was declassified from a higher appellation
The wine is too young to be given a year
The wine is not claimed as the produce of a single harvest
The wine was bottled before the year of the harvest could be established and confirmed by the authorities
exp: A year is a claim, and European rules allow it only where the fruit came overwhelmingly from the harvest named, with individual appellations free to demand the whole of it, so a wine drawing broadly on more than one picking cannot make that claim. Blending across years is a legitimate technique rather than a fault, and for such a wine the brand and the producer are what a buyer has to go on instead of a date.

q: Shelves carry two vintages of one wine and the labels are otherwise identical. What does the year on each reliably tell a buyer?
opts: Whether the wine will improve with further keeping in bottle
How long the wine spent in barrel
Whether the harvest was a good one
How old the wine is
exp: A vintage is a date and not a verdict. Whether a given year went well in a given place is knowledge the reader brings to the label, and readiness depends as much on the producer and the style as it does on the weather.

q: Solera 1888 is printed across a sherry label, and the wine inside was bottled last year. What does that date record?
opts: The year the solera was laid down
The year the house was founded
The year the youngest wine in the blend was picked
The year the bottle was filled
exp: A fractionally blended wine has no single harvest to declare, so the date points at the establishment of the system instead. It is a claim about lineage and continuity, and a reader who takes it for a vintage will be out by more than a century.

q: One bottle states 750 ml and another 75 cl, and both are ordinary full-size bottles. What is the difference between them?
opts: None; they are the same volume in different units
One figure is taken before corking and the other after
The centilitre bottle holds slightly less
The centilitre figure includes the volume of the punt
exp: Seven hundred and fifty millilitres and seventy-five centilitres are identical. European labels have conventionally used centilitres and American ones millilitres, so a shelf of imports shows both notations for exactly the same bottle.

q: The net contents line on a bottle reads 1.5 L, and the wine inside is the same as in the standard bottle beside it. What is that format called?
opts: A jeroboam
A methuselah
A magnum
A double magnum
exp: A magnum holds two standard bottles and is the first step up the ladder of large formats, above which the names and the volumes attached to them vary by region. More wine behind the same width of neck is the physical argument for magnums ageing more slowly, which is one of the few format claims with something behind it.

q: An unfamiliar white states eight percent alcohol and says nothing about sweetness anywhere on the bottle. What does the low figure most often signal?
opts: The wine lost alcohol during ageing
The wine has been through a malolactic fermentation
The wine was diluted with water before bottling
Fermentation was stopped with grape sugar still in the wine
exp: Sugar that never ferments never becomes alcohol, so a wine well under ten percent has usually kept some of it. The reading is not infallible, but where a label is silent on sweetness the strength is the most useful number on the bottle.

q: Sweetness is stated on every sparkling wine sold in Europe and on only some still wines. What accounts for the difference?
opts: Sugar content is obligatory for sparkling wine and optional for still wine
Sweetness in still wine cannot be measured reliably
The requirement applies only to sparkling wines that took their bubbles from a fermentation in the bottle
Sparkling wine is always sweetened after fermentation and still wine never is
exp: A sparkling wine can be moved a long way across the sweetness scale after its fermentation has finished, so a buyer is told where it landed. A still wine may declare sweetness and very often does not, which is why the alcohol figure and the origin do so much of the work at the table.
